standard_text: Apply the sums of interior angles of triangles and quadrilaterals to solve real-world and mathematical problems.

progression.narrative: 6.GM.2 asks students to apply two facts, that a triangle's interior angles total 180 degrees and a quadrilateral's total 360 degrees, to solve real-world and mathematical problems. The on-grade skills build in one line: name which shape you are in and its total, add the known angles, subtract to find the missing one, then stretch that routine to real contexts, to problems with no figure, and to compound shapes. Students who struggle here usually carry gaps from well below grade six. The most common blockers are grade 5 skills: telling a triangle from a quadrilateral and its special types, and adding or subtracting the decimal angle measures the harder problems use. Intervention should rebuild the grade 3 and 4 basics of what a degree, a right angle, and a whole-number sum are, then the grade 5 classification and decimal work, before returning to the angle-sum routine.

steps.rationale: The standard's two anchor facts. Nothing can be 'applied' until 180 belongs to triangles and 360 belongs to quadrilaterals -- with the two-triangles-inside picture so the pair can't swap.
The core application move: add the known angles in a labeled figure and subtract from the shape's total. Every later step reuses this routine.
The standard's explicit 'real-world problems' demand: find the shape inside the context, and read angles marked with symbols (the right-angle square) as well as numbers.
Mathematical problems without a figure: with two unknowns, the leftover is a budget the missing angles share, so students must test combinations instead of ending at one subtraction.
Application at DOK 2: use the angle sum as a test to verify or refute a claim, and explain the verdict -- the sum becomes evidence, not just a recipe.
The Above Proficiency demand: compound figures composed of triangles and quadrilaterals, where each sub-shape gets its own equation and split corners recombine.

skills.name: Recognize angles, right angles, and benchmark angle measures

prerequisite_skill.description: Recognize an angle as two rays from a common point and identify right angles.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: How many degrees is the square corner of a piece of paper?

skills.i_do_script: An angle is measured in degrees, and a few sizes come up again and again. A square corner, like the corner of this paper, is a right angle: exactly 90 degrees, and figures mark it with a small square instead of a number. Two right angles laid against each other make a straight line, which is 180 degrees. Four right angles around one point make a full turn, which is 360 degrees. Fold a corner of paper to see the 90, then open it flat along an edge to see the 180.

canonical_error.pattern: Does not read the small square as a known 90 degree angle.
canonical_error.example: In a triangle with one corner marked by a small square, the student says that corner has no measure.
canonical_error.why: The student expects every angle to show a number. The small square is the symbol for a right angle, so it always means exactly 90 degrees even when no number is printed.

skills.item_template: A single angle named or shown, or a benchmark turn. Student names the measure of a right angle, straight angle, or full turn, or reads the small-square right-angle mark. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: How many degrees is a right angle?
What symbol marks a right angle in a figure?
How many degrees is a straight angle (a straight line)?
How many degrees is a full turn all the way around a point?
Two right angles laid side by side form a straight line. How many degrees is that?
How many right angles fit in a full turn?
A corner of a triangle is marked with a small square. How many degrees is that corner?
Is a 90 degree angle acute, right, or obtuse?
How many degrees is half of a full turn?

redirect_script.prompt: The small square is a label. Every time you see it, write 90 next to that corner before you do anything else. A right angle is always 90 degrees.
redirect_script.praise: You turned the square into 90 degrees. Now the figure cannot hide an angle from you.

vocabulary.definition: An angle that measures exactly 90 degrees, marked in a figure with a small square.
A straight line seen as an angle, measuring 180 degrees, the same as two right angles.
The unit used to measure how open an angle is, written with a small circle like 90 degrees.

next_steps.if_fail: Practice naming right, acute, and obtuse angles on real objects like door corners, scissors, and clock hands (grade 4) before returning to labeled figures.

worked_example_script.text: Fold a square corner of paper. Hold it into the corner of your desk. Say: this is a right angle, 90 degrees.
How many of these folded corners fit along the straight edge of the desk?
Two right corners fill the straight edge, so a straight line is 90 plus 90, which is 180 degrees. Four corners fit all the way around a point, so a full turn is 360 degrees.
If a student thinks a wider looking opening must be more than 90, lay the folded corner on top of it to compare against a true right angle.
Your turn: a corner of a triangle is marked with a small square. How many degrees is it?

skills.name: Add and subtract multi-digit whole numbers fluently

prerequisite_skill.description: Fluently add and subtract multi-digit whole numbers, including subtracting from numbers that end in zero.

skills.i_do_script: Every missing-angle problem ends with the same arithmetic: add the angles you know, then subtract from 180 or 360. When the total ends in zero, counting up beats borrowing. Watch 360 - 275: from 275 up to 300 is 25, and from 300 up to 360 is 60, so the difference is 25 plus 60, which is 85. Draw the hops on an open number line so the two jumps are easy to see and add.

canonical_error.pattern: Regrouping slips when subtracting from 180 or 360, which end in zeros.
canonical_error.example: For 180 - 65 the student writes 125 instead of 115, losing a ten while borrowing across the zero.
canonical_error.why: Subtracting from a number that ends in zero forces borrowing in two places at once. Counting up from the smaller number avoids the borrow entirely.

skills.item_template: A bare whole-number addition or subtraction using 180, 360, or angle-sized numbers. Numeric response, no figure, no context.

redirect_script.stop: Let us check that by counting up.
redirect_script.prompt: Start at the number you subtracted and count up to the total. How much to the next hundred, then how much more to 180 or 360? Add the two hops.
redirect_script.praise: You counted up instead of borrowing, which is the fastest way when the big number ends in zero.

vocabulary.definition: The answer you get when you add numbers together.
The answer you get when you subtract one number from another.

next_steps.if_fail: Drill subtraction from 100 first, like 100 - 35 and 100 - 62, until counting up is automatic, then return to 180 and 360 (grade 3 to 4).

worked_example_script.text: Write 360 - 275. Draw an open number line with 275 on the left and 360 on the right.
About how big should the answer be, closer to 10, 100, or 300?
Count up in hops: 275 plus 25 reaches 300, then 300 plus 60 reaches 360. Add the hops: 25 plus 60 is 85.
If a student's answer is off by exactly 10, they borrowed wrong. Move them to counting up, which sidesteps the borrow.
Your turn: use counting up for 180 - 115. What is your first hop?

skills.name: Classify triangles and quadrilaterals by their sides and angles

prerequisite_skill.description: Sort two-dimensional figures by their number of sides and angles, and name triangles, quadrilaterals, and their special types.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: How many sides does a quadrilateral have, and is a square a quadrilateral?

skills.i_do_script: Before you can use 180 for a triangle or 360 for a quadrilateral, you have to name the shape. Count the sides: three straight sides is a triangle, four straight sides is a quadrilateral. Triangles have special types by their angles, a right triangle has one square corner and an equilateral triangle has three equal angles. Quadrilaterals also come in types: a square and a rectangle both have four right angles, and a rhombus and a trapezoid are quadrilaterals too. A special name does not remove a shape from its family, because every four sided figure is still a quadrilateral.

canonical_error.pattern: Thinks a shape with a special name, like a square or rectangle, is not a quadrilateral.
canonical_error.example: Says a square is not a quadrilateral because it is a square.
canonical_error.why: The student treats the special name and the general family as opposites. A square has four sides, so it is a quadrilateral, and so are rectangles, rhombuses, and trapezoids.

skills.item_template: A named or pictured shape. Student classifies it as a triangle or a quadrilateral, names its special type, or counts its sides and angles. Multiple choice or short response.

sample_items.stem: How many sides and how many angles does a triangle have?
How many sides and how many angles does a quadrilateral have?
Is a square a triangle or a quadrilateral?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students who think a special name removes a shape from its family pick neither; a square has 4 sides, so it is a quadrilateral.

sample_items.stem: A closed shape has 3 straight sides. What is it called?
sample_items.distractor_logic: The three quadrilateral options bait students who do not connect 3 sides to triangle.

sample_items.stem: Name the special triangle that has three equal sides and three equal angles.
How many right angles does a rectangle have?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students who picture only one square corner answer 1 or 2; a rectangle has four right angles.

sample_items.stem: Which shape is NOT a quadrilateral: square, trapezoid, triangle, or rhombus?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Square, trapezoid, and rhombus are all four sided; only the triangle has three sides.

sample_items.stem: A trapezoid has how many sides and angles?

redirect_script.prompt: Three sides is a triangle, four sides is a quadrilateral. Say the number of sides out loud, then name the family before you name the special type.
redirect_script.praise: You counted the sides and named the family. A square is still a quadrilateral, and it always will be.

vocabulary.definition: A closed shape with exactly 3 straight sides and 3 angles.
A closed shape with exactly 4 straight sides and 4 angles. Squares, rectangles, rhombuses, and trapezoids are all quadrilaterals.
A 90 degree angle, the square corner. A rectangle and a square each have four of them.

worked_example_script.text: Lay out cut-out shapes: a square, a right triangle, a trapezoid, and an equilateral triangle.
Point to each shape and count its straight sides out loud. Which pile does it go in, triangles or quadrilaterals?
Three sides go in the triangle pile, four sides go in the quadrilateral pile. The right triangle and the equilateral triangle are triangles, the square and the trapezoid are quadrilaterals.
If a student sets the square aside as not a quadrilateral, count its sides together: four sides means it belongs in the quadrilateral pile, special name and all.
Your turn: a shape has four straight sides. Triangle or quadrilateral?

practice_problems.stem: How many sides does a triangle have? How many does a quadrilateral have?
practice_problems.answer: A triangle has 3 sides; a quadrilateral has 4 sides.

practice_problems.stem: Is a rhombus a triangle or a quadrilateral?
practice_problems.answer: A quadrilateral, because it has 4 sides.

practice_problems.stem: Sort these into triangles and quadrilaterals: square, right triangle, trapezoid, equilateral triangle.
practice_problems.answer: Triangles: right triangle, equilateral triangle. Quadrilaterals: square, trapezoid.

practice_problems.stem: Marcus says a square cannot be a quadrilateral because it is a square. Is he right? Explain.
practice_problems.answer: No. A square has 4 sides, so it is a quadrilateral. Square is its special name, but it stays in the quadrilateral family.

practice_problems.stem: Name each triangle by its angles: one has a square corner, and another has three equal angles.
practice_problems.answer: The one with a square corner is a right triangle; the one with three equal angles is an equilateral triangle.

practice_problems.stem: Which special quadrilaterals have four right angles?
practice_problems.answer: A square and a rectangle.

practice_problems.stem: A diagonal is drawn across a rhombus from one corner to the opposite corner. How many triangles is it split into, and how many sides does each triangle have?
practice_problems.answer: Two triangles, each with 3 sides.

practice_problems.stem: A student sorted shapes and put the rectangle in the not a quadrilateral pile. Find the mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: The rectangle has 4 straight sides, so it is a quadrilateral. Only the triangle, with 3 sides, is not a quadrilateral.

activities.title: Sort by Sides
materials: A bag of cut-out shapes (triangles and quadrilaterals of many types)
Two labeled mats: Triangles and Quadrilaterals
activities.instructions:
1. Each pair empties the bag of shapes.
2. One partner picks a shape, counts its straight sides out loud, and places it on the correct mat.
3. The other partner checks: does the count match the mat?
4. Then sub-sort the Quadrilaterals mat into shapes with four right angles (squares, rectangles) and shapes without.
5. Say each time: I counted this many sides, so it is a triangle or a quadrilateral.

activities.title: Family or Not
materials: A deck of shape name cards
activities.instructions:
1. Shuffle the deck and flip one card, like square or triangle.
2. Players race to say whether the shape is a quadrilateral and give the reason: how many sides it has.
3. The first correct reason keeps the card.
4. Slip the special names (rhombus, rectangle, trapezoid) in often to catch anyone who forgets they are quadrilaterals.

strategy_links.why: Handling and sorting real cut-out shapes makes count the sides a physical move before the classification is named.
Sort and justify in pairs surfaces who is naming shapes from a memorized picture and who is actually counting sides.
Quick choral rounds of three sides, triangle and four sides, quadrilateral build the automatic sides to family pairing.

questioning_prompts: How many straight sides does this shape have? So which family is it in?
A square has its own name. Does that stop it from being a quadrilateral? Why not?
What makes a triangle a right triangle instead of just a triangle?
Which quadrilaterals have four right angles, and which do not?
If a shape has four straight sides, what do you already know about it?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student says a square or rectangle is not a quadrilateral.
misconception_redirects.say: Count its sides with me. Four straight sides means it is a quadrilateral, no matter what special name it also has.
misconception_redirects.praise: You kept the shape in its family. A square is always a quadrilateral.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student names a shape by how it is turned, like calling a tilted square a diamond in a different family.
misconception_redirects.say: Turn it back upright. Did any side disappear? The number of sides did not change, so the name did not change.
misconception_redirects.praise: You judged by the sides, not by the tilt.

quick_checks.prompt: Is a trapezoid a triangle or a quadrilateral?
quick_checks.look_for: Quadrilateral, with the reason that it has four sides.

quick_checks.prompt: How many right angles does a rectangle have?

worked_solution.stem: Classify this shape: it has 4 straight sides and 4 corners. Is it a triangle or a quadrilateral, and could it also have a special name?

steps.annotation: The number of sides names the family.
Every closed shape with four straight sides is a quadrilateral.

steps.math: special names: square, rectangle, rhombus, trapezoid
steps.annotation: If it also has four right angles it is a rectangle or square, but it is a quadrilateral either way.

faded_example.stem: Classify a shape that has 3 straight sides and one square corner.

steps.annotation: The number of sides names the family.
Every closed shape with three straight sides is a triangle.
The square corner is a right angle. What special triangle has a right angle?
State the full name of the shape.

sentence_starters: This shape has ___ straight sides, so it is a ___.
A square is a quadrilateral because ___.

skills.name: Add and subtract decimals to the hundredths

prerequisite_skill.description: Add and subtract decimals to hundredths by lining up place values.

skills.i_do_script: Decimals add and subtract place by place, so the decimal points must line up. For 90 - 47.5, write 90 as 90.0 so both numbers show a tenths place, line up the points, and subtract: 90.0 - 47.5 = 42.5. Lining up the points is really lining up the place values, ones under ones and tenths under tenths. On a hundredths grid or in money, tenths add to tenths and hundredths add to hundredths.

canonical_error.pattern: Right-aligns the digits instead of lining up the decimal points.
canonical_error.example: Computes 4.2 + 0.35 by stacking 42 over 35 and gets 0.77.
canonical_error.why: The student lines up the last digits like whole-number addition, which puts tenths under hundredths. Only matching place values can be added.

skills.item_template: Add or subtract two decimals to the hundredths, often angle-sized numbers. Numeric response, one renaming or an appended zero may be needed.

redirect_script.stop: Are the decimal points lined up?
redirect_script.prompt: Stack the numbers so the decimal points sit in one column, adding a zero if a place is empty. Then add or subtract each place.
redirect_script.praise: You lined up the places, so every digit landed where it belongs.

vocabulary.definition: The size a digit's position gives it: ones, tenths, hundredths.
The first place to the right of the decimal point; one tenth is 0.1.
Trade ten of one place for one of the next larger place, like ten tenths for one whole.

worked_example_script.text: Write 90 - 47.5 stacked, with 90 rewritten as 90.0 and the decimal points in one column.
Why can I write 90 as 90.0 without changing it?
Ninety and ninety point zero are the same amount. Now subtract place by place: 0 tenths minus 5 tenths needs a trade, so borrow one from the ones. The result is 42.5.
If a student stacks 47.5 under 90 by the last digit, ask what place each digit is in. Tenths cannot line up under ones.
Your turn: line up and solve 180 - 132.5.

practice_problems.stem: Mia wrote 4.2 + 0.35 = 0.77. Find the mistake and fix it.
shown_work: stacked 42 over 35 by the last digit
practice_problems.answer: She lined up the last digits instead of the decimal points. 4.20 + 0.35 = 4.55.

activities.title: Build It in Money
materials: Play money or drawn dollars, dimes, and pennies
activities.instructions:
1. Build 6.75 in money: 6 dollars, 7 dimes, 5 pennies.
2. Subtract 2.5 by taking away 2 dollars and 5 dimes, trading a dollar for ten dimes if a place runs short.
3. Write the stacked problem next to the money and match each trade to a regroup.
4. Repeat with 90 - 47.5, writing 90 as 90 dollars and trading down to subtract.
5. Say each time: dollars with dollars, dimes with dimes, pennies with pennies.

activities.title: Spot the Slide
materials: Worked-problem slips, half aligned and half misaligned
activities.instructions:
1. Deal the slips face down.
2. Flip one at a time and decide: were the decimal points lined up, or did a digit slide into the wrong place?
3. For each wrong slip, name the place that got mixed, like tenths added to hundredths, and fix it.
4. Sort the slips into Lined Up and Slid piles; the group must agree before sorting.

content.worked_problem: 4.2 + 0.35 stacked by the last digits gives 0.77
content.why: Right-aligning puts the 2 tenths under the 5 hundredths, so unlike places were added.

strategy_links.why: Money and hundredths grids make place-value alignment concrete before the line-up-the-points rule is named.
Thinking aloud while stacking makes the choice of which digit sits under which audible and checkable.
Sorting aligned against misaligned worked examples confronts the right-align bug directly.

questioning_prompts: What place is this digit in? What place is the digit under it?
Why can you write 90 as 90.0 without changing its value?
Where did the trade come from when you subtracted the tenths?
Estimate first: should 90 - 47.5 be more or less than 40?
How is trading a dollar for ten dimes the same as regrouping?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student right-aligns the digits and ignores the decimal points.
misconception_redirects.say: Build both numbers in money. Can pennies add to dimes? Line up the points so each place adds to its own kind.
misconception_redirects.praise: You matched place to place, so the answer came out true.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student subtracts the smaller digit from the larger regardless of order.
misconception_redirects.say: In 90 - 47.5 you cannot take 5 tenths from 0 tenths without trading. Trade one from the ones for ten tenths first.
misconception_redirects.praise: You regrouped instead of flipping the digits, which keeps the value honest.

quick_checks.look_for: 1.15, with the 8 tenths added to 3 tenths, not to 5 hundredths.

steps.annotation: Append a zero so both numbers show a tenths place.
Decimal points in one column put each place over its match.

steps.math: tenths: 0 - 5 needs a trade, borrow 1 from the ones for 10 tenths
steps.annotation: Ten tenths minus 5 tenths is 5 tenths.
Finish the whole-number places after the trade.

steps.math: line up the decimal points: 101.5 over 88.5
steps.annotation: Ones under ones, tenths under tenths.
Ten tenths make one whole; write 0 and carry 1.
Add the ones and tens with the carried 1.
State the sum.

sentence_starters: I lined up the decimal points so that ___ adds to ___.
I wrote ___ as ___ so both numbers show the same places.

skills.name: Identify the interior angle sums of triangles and quadrilaterals

prerequisite_skill.description: Name triangles and quadrilaterals by their number of sides and angles
prerequisite_skill.check_question: How many angles does a quadrilateral have?

skills.i_do_script: Draw any triangle and label its angles 60, 70, and 50. Add them out loud: 60 + 70 + 50 = 180. Then say the big idea: this isn't a coincidence -- EVERY triangle's three interior angles add to exactly 180 degrees, no matter how the triangle looks. Then draw a quadrilateral, split it with one diagonal into two triangles, and say: two triangles means 180 + 180, so every quadrilateral's four angles add to 360 degrees.

canonical_error.pattern: Swaps or mixes the two angle sums -- says a triangle's angles add to 360 or a quadrilateral's add to 180
canonical_error.example: Asked for the sum of the interior angles of a quadrilateral, the student answers 180 degrees
canonical_error.why: The student memorized '180 and 360' as a pair of facts without an anchor for which shape owns which number. Without the picture -- a quadrilateral is TWO triangles, so it gets double -- the two facts float free and swap under pressure.

skills.item_template: A recall question: 'What is the sum of the interior angles of any triangle (or quadrilateral)?' MC with 4 choices drawn from 90, 180, 270, 360, 540. No computation.

sample_items.stem: What is the sum of the interior angles of any triangle?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 360 is the quadrilateral sum (the swap); 90 confuses 'angle sum' with 'right angle'

sample_items.stem: What is the sum of the interior angles of any quadrilateral?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 180 is the triangle sum (the swap); 540 comes from adding a third 180

sample_items.stem: The figure shows a quadrilateral split by a dashed diagonal into two triangles. Which statement explains why the interior angles of a quadrilateral add to 360 degrees?
sample_items.answer: The diagonal makes two triangles, and 180 + 180 = 360
choices: The diagonal makes two triangles, and 180 + 180 = 360
A quadrilateral has four right angles, and 4 x 90 = 360
A quadrilateral is twice as wide as a triangle
The diagonal adds 180 degrees to the shape
sample_items.distractor_logic: 'Four right angles' only works for rectangles -- students overgeneralize from the most familiar quadrilateral

sample_items.stem: A triangle has angles that measure 95 degrees, 25 degrees, and 60 degrees. A quadrilateral has angles that measure 100 degrees, 80 degrees, 100 degrees, and 80 degrees. Which statement is true?
sample_items.answer: The triangle's angles sum to 180 degrees and the quadrilateral's sum to 360 degrees
choices: The triangle's angles sum to 180 degrees and the quadrilateral's sum to 360 degrees
Both shapes' angles sum to 180 degrees
Both shapes' angles sum to 360 degrees
The triangle's angles sum to 360 degrees and the quadrilateral's sum to 180 degrees
sample_items.distractor_logic: The full swap is the last choice; 'both 360' catches students who think all closed shapes total 360

vocabulary.definition: An angle on the inside of a shape, at one of its corners.
The total you get when you add all the angle measures together.
A closed shape with exactly 3 sides and 3 interior angles.
A closed shape with exactly 4 sides and 4 interior angles.

redirect_script.stop: Stop -- which shape are we in?
redirect_script.prompt: Count the sides of the shape first and say it out loud: 3 sides is a triangle, ONE triangle, 180. 4 sides is a quadrilateral -- draw one diagonal and count the triangles inside. Two triangles means how much?
redirect_script.praise: You anchored the number to the shape -- two triangles inside, so double 180. That fact is yours now.

practice_problems.stem: How many interior angles does a triangle have? How many does a quadrilateral have?
practice_problems.answer: A triangle has 3 interior angles; a quadrilateral has 4.

practice_problems.stem: Fill in the blanks: the interior angles of any triangle add to ___ degrees, and the interior angles of any quadrilateral add to ___ degrees.
A triangle has angles measuring 50 degrees, 60 degrees, and 70 degrees. Add them. What total do you get, and will EVERY triangle give that same total?
practice_problems.answer: 50 + 60 + 70 = 180 degrees. Yes -- every triangle's interior angles sum to 180 degrees.
practice_problems.notes: The add-and-see confirms the fact instead of just reciting it.

practice_problems.stem: Draw any quadrilateral and one diagonal. How many triangles did the diagonal make, and what does that tell you about the quadrilateral's angle sum?
practice_problems.answer: Two triangles; 180 + 180 = 360 degrees.
practice_problems.notes: This picture is the anchor that stops the 180/360 swap.

practice_problems.stem: True or false: a very long, skinny triangle has an angle sum bigger than 180 degrees because it's stretched out. Explain.
practice_problems.answer: False. Every triangle's interior angles sum to exactly 180 degrees no matter its size or shape.
practice_problems.notes: Targets the belief that size changes the sum.

practice_problems.stem: Marcus answered a quiz question. Find his mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Question: What is the sum of the interior angles of any quadrilateral?
Marcus wrote: 180 degrees, because shapes' angles always add to 180.
practice_problems.answer: The sum is 360 degrees. 180 is the TRIANGLE sum. A quadrilateral splits into two triangles, so its angles total 180 + 180 = 360 degrees.
practice_problems.notes: Baits the 180 vs 360 swap head-on.

practice_problems.stem: A pentagon (5 sides) can be split by diagonals from one corner into three triangles. Use the triangle fact to find the sum of a pentagon's interior angles.
practice_problems.answer: 3 x 180 = 540 degrees.
practice_problems.notes: Extends the two-triangle argument -- students who can do this OWN the quadrilateral fact.

practice_problems.stem: Explain to a 4th grader why a quadrilateral's angles add to 360 degrees, using only the triangle fact and a drawing.
practice_problems.answer: Draw a quadrilateral, connect two opposite corners with a diagonal. That makes two triangles. Each triangle's angles add to 180, and together the two triangles' angles make up all four corners of the quadrilateral, so 180 + 180 = 360.
practice_problems.notes: Reversed direction: produce the explanation, not just recognize it.

activities.title: Tear the Corners Off
materials: Paper triangles and quadrilaterals (2-3 per pair, cut in different shapes)
activities.instructions:
1. Each pair tears (or cuts) the three corners off a paper triangle.
2. They arrange the three corner pieces point-to-point along a straight line drawn on blank paper -- the pieces exactly fill the straight line (180 degrees).
3. Repeat with a quadrilateral's four corners arranged around a single point -- they fill a full turn (360 degrees).
4. Debrief question: why did skinny triangles and wide triangles BOTH fill the straight line exactly?

activities.title: 180 or 360?
activities.instructions:
1. Groups sort each card under the header 180 degrees or 360 degrees.
2. For each card, one student must say WHY before the card is placed -- 'it's a triangle, one triangle is 180.'
3. Debrief: which cards tried to trick you, and what saved you?

activities.title: Shape Sum Showdown
activities.instructions:
1. Call out a shape ('triangle!', 'quadrilateral!', 'square!', 'kite!') and students write its angle sum and hold boards up on the count of three.
2. Speed up as the class gets confident; sneak in repeats of 'triangle' right after 'quadrilateral' to catch autopilot swaps.
3. Any split in the room becomes a 30-second turn-and-convince before the next round.

strategy_links.why: Physically tearing corners and laying them on a straight line makes 180 a thing students SAW, not a fact they memorized.
Choral 'triangle -- 180! quadrilateral -- 360!' rounds build the automatic shape-to-sum pairing this skill lives on.
Turn-and-convince on 'why 360?' surfaces who has the two-triangles anchor and who is just reciting.

questioning_prompts: How many sides does this shape have -- and what does that tell you about its angle sum?
How many triangles can you cut a quadrilateral into with one diagonal? So what's its angle sum?
Does a bigger triangle have a bigger angle sum? Why not?
If I told you a shape's angles add to 360 degrees, could it be a triangle? How do you know?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student says a triangle's angles add to 360, or a quadrilateral's add to 180 -- the sums float free of the shapes.
misconception_redirects.say: Count the sides of the shape first and say it out loud: 3 sides is a triangle, ONE triangle, 180. 4 sides is a quadrilateral -- draw one diagonal and count the triangles inside. Two triangles means how much?
misconception_redirects.praise: You anchored the number to the shape -- two triangles inside, so double 180. That fact is yours now.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student says every quadrilateral's angles are each 90 degrees because squares are.
misconception_redirects.say: Draw me a quadrilateral that leans -- like a pushed-over square. Are those corners still 90? Add all four with an estimate: two got bigger, two got smaller. What stayed the same?
misconception_redirects.praise: Exactly -- the individual angles change, but the TOTAL stays locked at 360.

quick_checks.prompt: Fingers up: 1 finger if a triangle's angle sum is 180, 2 fingers if it's 360.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a triangle with angles labeled 60, 70, and 50. Below it, draw a quadrilateral with a dashed diagonal splitting it into two triangles.
Add the triangle's three angles for me. What do you get?
180 -- and here's the amazing part: EVERY triangle lands on exactly 180. Skinny ones, wide ones, right triangles. Always 180.

skills.name: Calculate the missing angle in a triangle or quadrilateral

prerequisite_skill.description: Know the angle sums: 180 degrees for a triangle, 360 for a quadrilateral (6GM2-S1)
prerequisite_skill.check_question: What do the interior angles of a quadrilateral add up to?

skills.i_do_script: Show a triangle with angles 55 degrees, 60 degrees, and x. Narrate the three-beat routine: ONE -- count the sides; three sides means the total is 180. TWO -- add what I know: 55 + 60 = 115. THREE -- subtract from the total: 180 - 115 = 65, so x = 65 degrees. Then check by adding all three: 55 + 60 + 65 = 180. The routine never changes; only the total does when the shape has four sides.

canonical_error.pattern: Uses the wrong total -- subtracts from 360 in a triangle or from 180 in a quadrilateral
canonical_error.example: For a triangle with angles 55 and 60, the student computes x = 360 - 55 - 60 = 245 instead of 180 - 55 - 60 = 65
canonical_error.why: The student has the subtraction routine down but skips the first decision -- which shape am I in? 360 is the 'angle number' they reach for by default, so every problem becomes a 360 problem. They aren't reading the figure before computing.

skills.item_template: A triangle (two known angles) or quadrilateral (three known angles) shown in a labeled figure, with the unknown marked x degrees. Student finds x. MC with 4 choices or NR. Whole-number measures; decimals at stretch only.

sample_items.stem: The figure below shows a triangle with the given angle measurements. What is the measurement of angle x?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 245 = 360 - 55 - 60 (wrong total); 115 = 55 + 60 (stopped after adding); 55 repeats a given angle

sample_items.stem: The figure below shows a quadrilateral with the given angle measurements. What is the measurement of angle x?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Spec-shaped item: 140 forgets one known angle when adding; 260 = 360 minus only 100; 40 subtracts from 180 (wrong total, then forced positive)

sample_items.stem: The figure below shows a right triangle. The right angle is marked with a small square. What is the measurement of angle x?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 128 = 180 - 52 (forgot the right angle); 52 repeats the given; 142 = 180 - 38 confuses which angle is unknown

sample_items.stem: The figure below shows a quadrilateral with one right angle marked with a small square. What is the measurement of angle x?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 165 = 360 - 90 - 105 (forgot the 90? no -- forgot the 105's partner: 360-90-105=165 forgets one angle); 285 subtracts only one angle; 105 repeats a given

sample_items.distractor_logic: Decimal (difficult tier): 132.5 forgets the right angle; 52.5 is a regrouping slip; 47.5 repeats the given

Add every angle you know -- all three of them. Cross each one off as you add it.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a triangle with angles labeled 55 degrees, 60 degrees, and x.

What do the two angles we know add up to?

Write: x = 180 - 115 = 65. Then write the check: 55 + 60 + 65 = 180.

skills.name: Solve real-world problems involving a missing interior angle

prerequisite_skill.description: Calculate a missing angle in a bare triangle or quadrilateral figure (6GM2-S2)
prerequisite_skill.check_question: A triangle has angles of 40 degrees and 60 degrees. What is the third angle?

skills.i_do_script: Show the ramp picture: a right triangle where the ground meets the wall at a square-marked corner, the ramp rises at 30 degrees, and the top angle is x. Narrate: the story is about a ramp, but the MATH is about a triangle. The square corner is 90 even though no number is printed. So x = 180 - 90 - 30 = 60 degrees. The whole skill is finding the triangle hiding inside the story -- especially the angles the picture marks with symbols instead of numbers.

canonical_error.pattern: Leaves out an angle the figure marks with a symbol instead of a number -- usually the small-square right angle
canonical_error.example: For a ramp shaped like a right triangle with a 28 degree rise, the student computes x = 180 - 28 = 152 instead of 180 - 90 - 28 = 62
canonical_error.why: Real-world figures often label the right angle with only the small square. The student scans for printed NUMBERS to subtract, and an angle with no digits next to it never enters the equation -- they subtract one angle and think they're done.

skills.item_template: A one-sentence real-world context (ramp, roof truss, sail, garden bed, tile, kite, frame) with a labeled triangle or quadrilateral figure; one angle is x. Student enters the missing measure in degrees. NR. Whole numbers at core; decimals at stretch.

sample_items.stem: A carpenter designs a ramp in the shape of a right triangle, as shown in the figure. The right angle is marked with a small square. Enter the measure, in degrees, of the missing angle x.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 120 (= 180 - 60) means the square-marked 90 was skipped; 210 means 360 was used as the total

sample_items.stem: A sail on a boat is shaped like a triangle, as shown in the figure. Two of its angles measure 64 degrees and 71 degrees. Enter the measure, in degrees, of the missing angle x.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 225 means 360 was used as the total; 135 (= 180 - 45?) no -- 116 or 109 mean only one known angle was subtracted

sample_items.stem: A floor tile is shaped like a quadrilateral, as shown in the figure. Three of its angles measure 102 degrees, 78 degrees, and 95 degrees. Enter the measure, in degrees, of the missing angle x.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 180 (= 360 - 102 - 78) means one known angle was forgotten; a negative-looking or tiny answer means 180 was used as the total

sample_items.stem: A window frame is shaped like a quadrilateral with two right angles at the bottom, each marked with a small square, as shown in the figure. The top-right angle measures 118 degrees. Enter the measure, in degrees, of the missing angle x.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 152 (= 360 - 90 - 118) means only one square-marked 90 was counted; 242 means both squares were ignored

practice_problems.stem: A kite is a quadrilateral. Three of its angles measure 100 degrees, 100 degrees, and 128 degrees. Find the fourth angle.

practice_problems.stem: A skateboard ramp is a right triangle. The ramp rises from the ground at 28 degrees, and the corner where the vertical support meets the ground is a right angle marked with a small square. Priya found the top angle x. Find her mistake and fix it.

practice_problems.notes: Baits the forgot-one-angle error: the square-marked 90 never entered her equation.

practice_problems.stem: A tabletop is a quadrilateral with angles measuring 90 degrees (marked with a small square), 115 degrees, and 85 degrees. Find the fourth angle.
practice_problems.notes: The 90 is described by its square -- checks the symbol-to-number habit in word form.

practice_problems.stem: A ramp is shaped like a right triangle. The ramp surface makes an angle of 22.5 degrees with the ground. What is the angle at the top of the ramp?
practice_problems.notes: Decimal computation is the spec's difficult tier.

practice_problems.stem: Design your own: describe a real object shaped like a quadrilateral, give three of its angles (make one a right angle you describe only with the small square), and show how to find the fourth.
practice_problems.answer: Answers vary. Example: a picture frame with a square-marked corner (90), plus 105 and 80; fourth angle = 360 - 90 - 105 - 80 = 85 degrees. All four angles must total 360.
practice_problems.notes: Producing the problem forces students to encode the square symbol themselves.

activities.instructions:

content.worked_problem: A wheelchair ramp is a right triangle: the ground and the vertical post meet at a square-marked corner, and the ramp rises at 32 degrees. Deshawn wrote: x = 180 - 32 = 148 degrees.
content.error_step: Deshawn subtracted only the 32 -- the square-marked right angle never entered his equation.
content.why: The small square IS a label: it means exactly 90 degrees. A triangle has THREE angles, so the equation needs three: x = 180 - 90 - 32 = 58 degrees. Counting the corners you subtracted (there should be one fewer than the shape's sides... actually: every corner except x) catches this instantly.

1. Flash a figure card. Student 1 writes ONLY the total (180 or 360). Student 2 adds the known angles -- including any square corners. Student 3 finishes the subtraction.

quick_checks.look_for: Two -- 90 and 40 (then x = 50). A student who says 'one' is square-blind; send them back to touching corners.

steps.annotation: The story is about a ramp, but the math is about a triangle. Three sides means 180.

Forget ramps for a second -- what SHAPE do you see, and what must its angles total?
Touch each corner with me. This one says 30. This one has no number at all -- just a little square. What is it telling us?
